newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea renews call for talks, apology from North.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea renews call for talks, apology from North.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Wednesday renewed demands for an apology from North Korea for a recent submarine incursion and suggested help for Pyongyang once it agreed to serious talks with his country.
"North Korea should quickly wake up from the wild fantasy that it can resolve all problems through direct dialogue with the United States," Kim told South Korean reporters.
The remarks by Kim, who is visiting Malaysia, were broadcast in South Korea by state radio and television networks.
"North Korea should realise that it is virtually impossible to resolve its food problems or build light-water nuclear reactors without South-North (Korean) dialogue," he said.
Seoul has said it will provide economic assistance to Pyongyang once it agreed to detente.

North Korea, suffering from a severe food shortage after heavy rains and floods this year and in 1995, halted its suspected arms program in return for two light-water reactors and interim energy supplies in a deal worth about $4.5 billion.
Under the 1994 accord, Washington promised to provide Pyongyang with the reactors and alternative supplies if the North froze the weapons program.
South Korea has said it will pay the lion's share of the reactors but recently delayed sending technicians to do site work preparation in the North.
The delay came after tensions rose between the two Koreas after a Northern submarine landed 26 agents on a South Korean beach in September.
All but two of the North Korean agents from the submarine were shot dead. One was captured alive and another is still at large.
Kim said South Korea could not put the submarine incident behind it unless Pyongyang apologised and assured such provocation would not be repeated.

He said the communist North had previously sent armed spies to the South many times but this was the first time a squad of commandos comprising officers was dispatched by submarine, which Kim called an offensive weapon.
"This is a kind of an act of war and an obvious, serious violation of the armistice agreement and the basic treaty agreement of the South and North," he said.

The armistice agreement halted the 1950-53 Korean War while the basic treaty, which included a non-aggression agreement, was signed in 1991 during a rare blossoming of goodwill between the Cold War rivals.
The North insists the submarine incident was an accident and has demanded the return of the bodies and the captured agent.
Kim and U.S. President Bill Clinton on Sunday called on Pyongyang to take unspecified "acceptable steps" to end a crisis caused by the submarine incursion.

Clinton and Kim, meeting in the Philippines during the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, also urged North Korea to accept four-nation peace talks to defuse tension on the Korean peninsula.

The two leaders jointly proposed the four-nation talks in April, inviting North Korea and China to join a dialogue aimed at replacing the truce that ended the 1950-53 war with a lasting peace. North Korea has not agreed to take part.
